newsitem.title: CANADA: Analysts see no Abitibi, Stone merger.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see no Abitibi, Stone merger.

text.p: Analysts said on Tuesday they saw no immediate likelihood of a merger between Abitibi-Price Inc and Stone-Consolidated Corp, despite market rumors that the two companies had been in talks of some kind.

There has been speculation that Toronto-based Abitibi and Montreal-based Stone-Consolidated, which is 47 percent-owned by Stone Container Corp, of Chicago, may merge their companies or consolidate some of their newsprint mills in Quebec through a joint venture.
"I don't think it's going to happen," said an analyst who declined to be identified.
"It's a rumor," Stone-Consolidated spokeswoman Denise Dallaire told Reuters. An Abitibi spokesman could not be reached for comment.

On the Toronto Stock Exchange, neither Abitibi nor Stone-Consolidated shares were active on the speculation, which peaked on Monday when Stone-Consolidated indicated it planned a midday press release and then cancelled it.
On Tuesday afternoon, Abitibi shares were off 0.25 to 21.85, while Stone-Consolidated was down 0.10 to 20.55, both in thin trading. In New York, Stone Container was up 1/8 to 13-3/8.

Speculation of a merger between Abitibi and Stone-Consolidated has been driven by market expectations of a consolidation in eastern Canada's newsprint industry and in western Canada's pulp and paper sector.
"We know that there will be a consolidation in the industry," ScotiaMcLeod Inc analyst Richard Saucier said.

At about US$500 a metric ton in the eastern United States, newsprint prices are at what analysts see as rock bottom for the current price cycle. Several major producers plan price increases of US$75 a tonne for March 1 and most analysts expect prices to recover in the second half.

But the newsprint industry is struggling with too much capacity, particularly at older mills in eastern Canada. Two Abitibi newsprint mills that have been the subject of sale speculation -- at Chandler and Jonquiere, Quebec -- have not earned the company's "cornerstone" facility designation that would help ensure their future.
Analysts said Abitibi had been seeking to sell one or both of the Quebec mills, but that it was unlikely Stone-Consolidated would buy the facilities and invest the money needed to upgrade them.
Stone-Consolidated has been a good cash producer for Stone Container and analysts said its Chicago parent would not want to leverage the Canadian subsidiary further.

In a conference call with analysts on Tuesday to discuss fourth-quarter results, Stone Container chief executive Roger Stone gave little sign that the company was seeking to sell or merge Stone-Consolidated with another company, but said it received occasional expressions of interest in the unit.
